papers.title: PMB-NN: Physiological-Model-Based Neural Network for Glucose Forecasting in Type 1 Diabetes
papers.abstract: Accurate, physiologically consistent glucose forecasts could help people with type 1 diabetes respond to impending excursions. We applied our physiological-model-based neural network (PMB--NN) framework to glucose forecasting. A temporal convolutional network (TCN) used 180 min of history, constrained during training by a personalized four-parameter physiological model. The main PMB--NN combined forecast and neural--physiological agreement losses; a three-term variant additionally fitted physiological predictions to measured glucose. Data comprised 6--8 weeks of continuous glucose monitoring, pump, and meal records from 25 AZT1D participants. Person-specific models used chronological 70/10/20 train/validation/test splits and 30-, 60-, and 120-min horizons. Median mean absolute errors were 16.24, 25.00, and 30.20 mg/dL with basal insulin records and 15.38, 24.21, and 31.79 mg/dL before these records became available. In the latter setting, PMB--NN had the lowest median error at 30 and 60 min; it outperformed the physiological model alone in all six settings. In input-increase tests, glucose predictions changed in the expected direction for 85\% of correction boluses and 100\% of carbohydrate rescues, versus 57\% for active insulin and 56\% for active carbohydrates. Most standalone physiological fits showed locally distinguishable parameter effects, with glucose-related coefficients more stable under resampling than insulin- or carbohydrate-related coefficients. The three-term variant improved hyperglycaemia accuracy with basal records, but did not significantly change overall MAE and reduced directional plausibility in three tests. PMB--NN combines personalized forecasting with an explicit physiological model, allowing assessment of predictive accuracy, physiological response behavior, and participant-specific coefficients.

papers.title: Integrated Open-Source Framework for Simulation of Transcatheter Pulmonary Valves in Native Right Ventricular Outflow Tracts
papers.abstract: Pulmonary insufficiency is a consequence of transannular patch repair in Tetralogy of Fallot (ToF), leading to late morbidity and mortality. Transcatheter native outflow tract pulmonary valve replacement (TPVR) has become common, but assessment of patient candidacy and selection of the optimal device remains challenging. We demonstrate an integrated open-source workflow for simulation of TPVR in image-derived models to inform device selection. Machine learning-based segmentation of Computer Tomography (CT) scans was implemented to define the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT). A custom workflow for device positioning and pre-compression was implemented in SlicerHeart. Resulting geometries were exported to FEBio for simulation. Visualization of results and quantification were performed using custom metrics implemented in SlicerHeart and FEBio. RVOT model creation and device placement could be completed in under 1 minute. Virtual device placement using FE simulations visually mimicked actual device placement and allowed quantification of vessel strain, stress, and contact area. Regions of higher strain and stress were observed at the proximal and distal end locations of the TPVs where the devices impinge on the RVOT wall. No other consistent trends were observed across simulations. The observed variability in mechanical metrics across RVOTS, stents, and locations in the RVOT highlights that no single device performs optimally in all anatomies, thereby reinforcing the need for simulation-based patient-specific assessment. This study demonstrates the feasibility of a novel open-source workflow for the rapid simulation of TPVR, which, with further refinement, may inform assessment of patient candidacy and optimal device selection.

papers.title: Effect of Right Ventricular Outflow Tract Material Properties on Simulated Transcatheter Pulmonary Placement
papers.abstract: FE simulations emulating TPV system deployment in patient-specific right ventricular outflow tracts (RVOT) assume material properties for the RVOT and adjacent tissues. Sensitivity of the deployment to variation in RVOT material properties is unknown. Moreover, the effect of a transannular patch stiffness and location on simulated TPV deployment has not been explored. A sensitivity analysis on the material properties of a patient-specific RVOT during TPV deployment, modeled as an uncoupled HGO material, was conducted using FEBioUncertainSCI. Further, the effects of a transannular patch during TPV deployment were analyzed by considering two patch locations and four patch stiffnesses. Visualization of results and quantification were performed using custom metrics implemented in SlicerHeart and FEBio. Sensitivity analysis revealed that the shear modulus of the ground matrix (c), fiber modulus (k1), fiber dispersion (kappa), and fiber mean orientation angle (gamma) had the greatest effect on 95th%ile stress, whereas only c had the greatest effect on 95th%ile Lagrangian strain. First-order sensitivity indices contributed the greatest to the total-order sensitivity indices. Simulations using a transannular patch revealed that peak stress and strain were dependent on patch location and the underlying vessel geometry, with increasing patch stiffness modulating the magnitude of local stress concentrations. As stiffness of the patch increased, greater stress was observed at the interface connecting the patch to the RVOT, and stress in the patch itself increased while strain decreased. The total enclosed volume by the TPV device remained unchanged across all simulated patch cases. This study highlights that while uncertainties in tissue material properties and patch locations may influence functional outcomes, FE simulations provide a reliable framework for evaluating these outcomes in TPVR.

papers.title: Angle-domain null subtraction imaging from beamformed plane-wave data
papers.abstract: Null subtraction imaging (NSI) narrows the apparent lateral response by combining fields produced with a zero-mean apodization and two DC-offset variants. Usually, NSI requires channel data and flexible beamformers (Receive-NSI). We investigate Angle-NSI, which operates on per-angle images during coherent plane-wave compounding. A matrix formulation was used to distinguish receive-domain and angle-domain null subtraction expressions. The method was evaluated using a simulated point target, experimental resolution phantom targets, an open microbubble (MB) traces dataset and two in vivo carotid acquisitions. Angle sampling, noise, phase jitter and target position were swept in simulation. A synchronized GPU benchmark compared the complete reconstructions. Six beamforming methods were compared: delay-and-sum (DAS), coherence-factor-weighted DAS (CF-DAS), minimum variance beamforming (MV), delay-multiply-and-sum (DMAS), Receive-NSI and Angle-NSI. Angle-NSI reduced the simulated -6 dB lateral width from 0.226 mm for DAS to 0.116 mm, compared with 0.009 mm for Receive-NSI, while the axial width was 0.720 mm for these three methods. The lateral narrowing was confirmed on an experimental resolution phantom. Angle-NSI had shorter reconstruction time than Receive-NSI and the lowest post-delay processing time among the nonlinear methods. In power Doppler, microbubble trace widths were reduced by 50.2% for Receive-NSI and 30.9% for Angle-NSI compared to DAS. On a phantom and in vivo, both NSI variants reduced generalized contrast-to-noise ratio relative to the conventional methods. Angle-NSI provides simple post-processing of per-angle beamformed images. It narrows the apparent lateral response at low computational cost, at the expense of B-mode detectability: this makes it a well-suited alternative for high-resolution power Doppler applications.
